records.content: Blending Combining liquids from different batches, vintages, varieties or cask types in set proportions to stabilise quality, balance structure or build a fixed style; wine, Champagne, whisky, brandy and baijiu follow different rules and logics. Blending Blending is the process of combining liquids from different batches, vintages, varieties, regions or cask types in set proportions. It can be a technical tool for consistency or the core of style design. Wine, Champagne, whisky, brandy and baijiu all blend, but the permitted scope, terminology and goals differ. Reading blending as simply "mixing things together" ignores proportional design, sensory calibration and the settling that follows.

records.content: Distillation A process that separates and concentrates ethanol from a fermented liquid or mash by exploiting differences in boiling points; equipment, reflux and cut points shape the spirit's flavour. Distillation Distillation separates ethanol from water and other volatile components by exploiting differences in boiling points. Fermented liquid or mash usually contains only a low concentration of ethanol; heating, vaporisation and condensation produce a distillate with higher alcohol strength. records.content: Fermentation The metabolic process in which yeast or bacteria convert sugar into ethanol, carbon dioxide and flavour compounds under low oxygen; strain, temperature, sugar concentration, pH and oxygen set speed, strength and aroma. Fermentation Fermentation is the metabolic process in which yeast or bacteria break down sugar under low-oxygen conditions and produce ethanol, carbon dioxide and flavour compounds. It converts the chemical energy of sugar into cellular energy and releases ethanol as a waste product. records.content: Fortification The addition of grape spirit to wine to raise alcohol and stabilise the wine; fortifying mid-fermentation retains residual sugar, while fortifying after fermentation gives a dry fortified style, so timing and proportion decide the result. Fortification Fortification is the addition of distilled spirit to wine. The spirit is usually grape-derived alcohol or brandy, and the aim is to raise the alcohol of the finished wine, suppress microbial activity, stabilise the wine and, in the process, retain sugar or shape flavour. Fortified wine is a category of its own precisely because this step rewrites where fermentation ends, rather than merely raising an alcohol number. Fortification

Kimoto keeps the yamafuri step, in which the mixture is mashed into a paste, while yamahai omits it. Lagering Lagering sits after primary fermentation and before filtration and filling. The German verb lagern means "to store", and the stage places the beer in conditions close to freezing so that yeast metabolism, colloidal settling and carbonation can finish slowly. Lees ageing Lees ageing (French sur lie) keeps wine in contact with the lees that settle after fermentation. The bulk of the lees is spent yeast, mixed with a little grape debris and tartrate. Gross lees are coarse and prone to spoilage and are usually separated quickly; fine lees are small, slow to settle and may deliberately be retained. records.content: Malolactic fermentation A secondary fermentation in which lactic acid bacteria convert malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide; it lowers titratable acidity, raises pH and softens texture, adding creamy notes in moderation but volatile acidity, biogenic amines and haze when uncontrolled. Malolactic fermentation Malolactic fermentation, shortened to MLF, is a secondary fermentation in wine. It is often confused with alcoholic fermentation, but the agents differ completely: alcoholic fermentation uses yeast to turn sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide, while malolactic fermentation uses lactic acid bacteria to turn malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide and produces no alcohol.

records.title: Malting

records.content: Malting The pre-treatment that steeps, germinates, kilns and de-roots barley and other grains; the degree of germination and the kilning curve set amylase power, modification and colour, and therefore saccharification efficiency and finished flavour. Malting Malting turns barley and other grains into malt. Its core is not simply letting grain sprout: germination wakes the grain's own enzyme system, and kilning then fixes those enzymes and drives moisture down. Beer and whisky both depend on malting, because without the amylases supplied by malt, saccharification cannot convert endosperm starch into fermentable sugar. Malting image Figure: Malting. records.content: Oak ageing Storing wine or spirit in oak casks so that wood, trace oxygen and time change aroma, tannin, colour and texture; species, cask size, age and toast level are adjustable variables. Oak ageing Oak ageing means storing wine or spirit in oak casks for a period so that wood, oxygen and time change the drink together. It is not simply "putting it in a barrel" but a set of adjustable variables: oak species, cask size, age, toast level, ageing environment and duration all affect the final style. records.content: Pressing Pressing separates juice or wine from skins, seeds and stems. White wines are usually pressed before fermentation, red wines after maceration or fermentation, and the pressure curve and fraction cuts decide yield, tannin and body. Pressing Pressing separates juice or wine from skins, seeds and stems. It looks like simple squeezing, but it is a trade-off over pressure, time and fraction cuts: more pressure raises yield but also pulls in tannin, colour and bitterness; less pressure gives cleaner liquid but lower volume. records.content: Qu making A traditional process that cultures moulds, yeasts and bacteria on grain to make a saccharifying and fermenting starter; qu quality and microbial community directly affect yield and flavour in baijiu and yellow wine. Qu making Qu making is a key step in traditional Chinese brewing: culturing microbes on grain to make a saccharifying and fermenting starter. Qu is not a single yeast but a carrier on which moulds, yeasts and bacteria grow together; it both breaks starch down into sugar and takes part in fermentation and aroma production. Baijiu, yellow wine and some other grain drinks depend on qu, but the qu types and processes differ. Qu making image Figure: Qu making. Image: Uranas

records.content: Saccharification The process that breaks starch in grains and other raw materials into fermentable sugars; malt enzymes, mould enzymes from qu, temperature, pH and the water-to-grain ratio set the sugar profile and shape body, yield and fermentation. Saccharification Saccharification breaks grain starch into sugars that yeast can use. Starch is a polymer of glucose, and its granules are wrapped in protein and lipid, so pitching yeast directly onto grain ferments almost nothing. Only after gelatinisation and enzymatic hydrolysis into glucose, maltose and maltotriose can the sugar enter fermentation. records.content: Stacked fermentation An open process step in baijiu production in which qu-inoculated mash is piled for a period before pit loading, allowing natural warming and microbial multiplication. records.content: Bavaria A federal state in southern Germany and one of the world's most famous beer-law territories. Munich, Nuremberg, Bamberg and Bayreuth each have a clear brewing tradition, from pale lager to smoked beer, wheat beer and strong doppelbock. Its water is medium-hard, not purely soft. Fushimi Fushimi is a sake region in the southern part of Kyoto City, centred on the brewery cluster that runs along the Uji River and the Horikawa canal in Fushimi ward. It is not a separate prefecture, nor a vineyard-style legal appellation. Its reputation rests on the Fushui spring water, brewery architecture, and a shipping history that made sake a visible part of the city.

The Gan River runs through the province from south to north. Red soils, hills, rice fields and abundant rain create a classic Jiangnan agricultural landscape and a long base for rice-based brewing. The province's most distinctive baijiu coordinate is Site and te-aroma. records.content: Marlborough Marlborough wine region at the north-east end of New Zealand's South Island, the country's largest. records.content: Pauillac A red-wine AOC on the left bank of the Gironde in the middle Médoc, recognised on 14 November 1936, with about 1,250 hectares of vines on Quaternary gravel terraces roughly ten metres thick; the 1855 classification lists Lafite Rothschild, Latour and Mouton Rothschild as first growths here, and the rules set a minimum natural alcohol of 11%, a yield of 57 hl/ha with a ceiling of 63 hl/ha, and a minimum planting density of 7,000 vines per hectare. Pauillac Pauillac is a red-wine appellation on the left bank of the Gironde estuary, in the middle of the Médoc peninsula in the Gironde department of France, recognised as an AOC on 14 November 1936. records.summary: A Bordeaux left-bank AOC split from Graves in 1987, covering ten communes south of the city; known for gravel mounds, both red and white wines and estates such
records.content: Pessac-Léognan A Bordeaux left-bank AOC split from Graves in 1987, covering ten communes south of the city; known for gravel mounds, both red and white wines and estates such as Haut-Brion and La Mission Haut-Brion, it is Bordeaux’s most urban and accessible fine-wine district. Pessac-Léognan Pessac-Léognan lies south of Bordeaux city, the northern section of the Graves district that became an independent AOC in 1987. On gravel ridges it makes both red and white wines: reds are Bordeaux blends led by Cabernet Sauvignon, whites blend Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, and the district ranks among the most respected sources of dry white wine in Bordeaux. Pfalz Pfalz is the German appellation that runs along the German Wine Route from Bockenheim to Schweigen on the Alsace border, 85 kilometres in length and linking about 130 villages. records.title: Piedmont
records.summary: A wine region in north-west Italy framed by the Alps and the Langhe and Monferrato hills; represented by Barolo and Barbaresco from Nebbiolo, Barbera and Moscat
records.content: Piedmont A wine region in north-west Italy framed by the Alps and the Langhe and Monferrato hills; represented by Barolo and Barbaresco from Nebbiolo, Barbera and Moscato d'Asti, with autumn fog (nebbia), hillside soils and strict DOCG ageing rules defining its style. Piedmont Piedmont (Italian Piemonte) lies in north-west Italy, bounded by the Alps to the north and west, Liguria to the south and Lombardy to the east. It is one of Italy's leading fine red-wine regions, centred on Nebbiolo, while Barbera, Dolcetto and Moscato complete a varied range of varieties. Piedmont photograph Figure: Piedmont. Porto Porto is a sweet fortified-wine appellation produced in the Douro valley of Portugal and aged in Vila Nova de Gaia or the Douro. records.title: Portugal
records.summary: A wine-producing country in the west of the Iberian Peninsula, known for fortified wines such as Port and Madeira and for Douro reds; native varieties are abund
records.content: Portugal A wine-producing country in the west of the Iberian Peninsula, known for fortified wines such as Port and Madeira and for Douro reds; native varieties are abundant and the appellation system is aligned with the EU framework. Portugal Portugal lies in the west of the Iberian Peninsula and has a deep wine tradition. Its international image is often tied to fortified wines such as Port and Madeira, but Portugal also makes Douro reds, warm Alentejo styles, fresh Vinho Verde whites and crisp rosés. Native varieties are abundant and are the key to understanding Portuguese wine. Portugal category image Figure: Portugal. Photograph: Porto-Matosinhos, , June 2 (53870205083). Credit: John Hay

records.content: Priorat An inland mountain region in Tarragona province, Catalonia, Spain, awarded DOQ status in 2009; steep terraces of llicorella slate and quartz, low-yielding old vines and a transitional Mediterranean-continental climate produce Grenache- and Carignan-led reds with full body and a mineral edge. Priorat Priorat (Spanish Priorato) is a mountain wine region inland in Tarragona province, Catalonia, in north-eastern Spain, enclosed by ranges of hills. It was granted DOQ (Denominació d'Origen Qualificada) status in 2009, making it one of only two top-tier origin names in Spain alongside Rioja. records.title: Provence
records.summary: A wine region on the Mediterranean coast of south-east France, running from the Rhône delta to west of Nice; best known for rosé, it also makes red and white wi
records.content: Provence A wine region on the Mediterranean coast of south-east France, running from the Rhône delta to west of Nice; best known for rosé, it also makes red and white wines, mainly from Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah and Mourvèdre, with Bandol and other appellations under their own rules. Provence Provence is the wine region most easily defined by the word "rosé", and also one of the most obscured by it. Its coast runs from the Rhône delta to west of Nice, with vineyards on limestone hills, schist slopes and coastal plains. Rosé is indeed dominant, but the Mourvèdre reds of Bandol, the whites of Cassis and the rare blends of Palette are the way into the region's depth. Provence is not a single st

records.content: Puglia Italy’s heel, shaped by Mediterranean sun, limestone and red soils, old vines and masserie farm estates; Negroamaro, Primitivo and Bombino Nero dominate, with the Salento peninsula and Manduria as the core. Puglia Puglia, known in English as Apulia, forms the heel of the Italian peninsula, with coasts on both seas. Mediterranean sun, limestone and red soils, old bush vines and masseria farm estates shape its image; Negroamaro, Primitivo and Bombino Nero lead the reds, with the Salento peninsula and Manduria at the core. records.summary: A wine region along the Rhône in south-eastern France, running from Vienne to Avignon; the north is a narrow band of steep slopes where reds are made from Syrah
records.content: Rhône Valley A wine region along the Rhône in south-eastern France, running from Vienne to Avignon; the north is a narrow band of steep slopes where reds are made from Syrah alone, the south is a broad valley where reds are Grenache-led blends, and the mistral blows through the whole region. Rhône Valley The Rhône Valley is a wine region along the Rhône in south-eastern France, running from Vienne south to Avignon. The north is a narrow band of steep slopes and the south is a broad valley, and the two differ markedly in climate, soils, varieties and rules while together forming France's second largest wine region band. records.content: Rías Baixas Wine DO in Galicia, north-west Spain, based mainly in Pontevedra. It began in 1980 as the Denominación Específica Albariño and became Rías Baixas in 1988; it has five sub-zones, Val do Salnés, Condado do Tea, O Rosal, Soutomaior and Ribeira do Ulla. The legal area lies below 300 metres, with about 4,320 hectares (10,677 acres), around 6,500 growers, more than 22,800 plots and some 180 registered wineries; maximum yields are 12,500 kg per hectare (90 hectolitres per hectare), and Albariño dominates. records.content: Ribera del Duero A wine appellation along the Duero river in Castilla y León, Spain, based on Tempranillo, known locally as Tinto Fino; vineyards sit on a high plateau at about 700–1000 metres in an extreme continental climate, and the reds are known for structure, ripe fruit and oak ageing, classified as Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva. records.content: Rueda White-wine DO in Castilla y León, Spain, granted official status on 12 January 1980 and the autonomous community's first DO. Its area covers 74 municipalities in Valladolid, Segovia and Ávila. Vineyards sit at 700–870 metres, annual rainfall is only 300–500 litres per square metre and sunshine reaches 2,600 hours a year. Verdejo dominates, at 88.82% of the 2025 harvest; gravel terraces and a wide day-night range shape the high-acid, herbal and citrus style. Rueda Rueda is a white-wine denomination in Castilla y León, Spain, on the high plains of the upper Duero. records.content: Saint-Émilion A wine region north-east of Libourne on Bordeaux's Right Bank, with 5400 hectares across 9 communes; Merlot is about 60%, the Saint-Émilion AOC caps yield at 46 hectolitres per hectare, the Grand Cru AOC at 40 with 12 months' ageing, and the 2022 classification lists 85 estates. Saint-Émilion Saint-Émilion is the Bordeaux Right Bank region most easily hidden by its classification. People remember the list that began in 1955 and overlook two more basic appellation rules: the Saint-Émilion AOC and the Saint-Émilion Grand Cru AOC. Sancerre Sancerre is a hill district in the eastern Loire, on the left bank of the Cher, known for Sauvignon Blanc whites and Pinot Noir reds and rosés. Santa Barbara County Santa Barbara County sits on California's southern Central Coast, where east-west ranges pull Pacific fog and cool air inland. Sub-AVAs such as Sta. Rita Hills, Santa Ynez Valley, Ballard Canyon and Happy Canyon are known for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Syrah; the county became an AVA in 1983 and is central to California's cool-climate discussion. records.content: Santorini PDO on the volcanic island of Santorini (Thira) in the Cyclades, Greece, established in 1971. Its dry white must contain at least 85% Assyrtiko, with the remaining 15% limited to Athiri and Aidani. Vineyards cover about 1,200 hectares (12,000 stremmata), from sea level to about 300 metres. Volcanic ash and pumice, extreme drought and the meltemia winds force the kouloura basket system. Maximum yields have been cut from 8,000 to 6,500 kg per hectare; Vinsanto and Nykteri are protected traditional terms. records.content: Sauternes The botrytised sweet white appellation of southern Bordeaux, covering the villages of Sauternes, Barsac, Bommes, Fargues and Preignac; autumn fog on the Ciron, gravel terraces and the 1855 classification define its identity. Sauternes Sauternes is the botrytised sweet white appellation of southern Bordeaux, in the Gironde, covering the villages of Sauternes, Barsac, Bommes, Fargues and Preignac. It is not one uniform tract of land but a set of terraces, gravel slopes and clay hollows along the Ciron and the Garonne. records.content: Savoie A wine region in the French Alps of south-east France, with vineyards on valleys and slopes at 250-600 metres; known for white varieties such as Jacquère and Altesse and the red Mondeuse, with appellations including Vin de Savoie, Roussette de Savoie, Crémant de Savoie and Bugey. Savoie Savoie is not a region that can be summed up with an Alpine view. Its vineyards are scattered across valleys, slopes and glacial terraces in south-east France, from 250 metres up to more than 600 metres; two sides of the same mountain can differ completely in soil, aspect and ripening date. records.title: Scotland
records.summary: A legally defined whisky region in the north of the United Kingdom; Scotch whisky must be distilled and matured in Scotland, aged in oak casks for at least thre
records.content: Scotland A legally defined whisky region in the north of the United Kingdom; Scotch whisky must be distilled and matured in Scotland, aged in oak casks for at least three years, bottled at no less than 40% ABV and protected by a geographical indication. Scotland Scotland lies in the north of the United Kingdom and is the legal home of Scotch whisky. Scotch is not just a drink but a protected name and process system: it must be distilled and matured in Scotland, made from water, malted barley (other cereals may be used) and yeast, aged in oak casks for at least three years, and bottled at no less than 40% ABV. records.content: Shaoxing The core huangjiu region in northern Zhejiang, on the south shore of Hangzhou Bay. Russian River Valley and Sonoma Coast are known for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, Alexander Valley for Cabernet Sauvignon, Dry Creek Valley for Zinfandel. European grapes were recorded in 1817 and 99% of vineyard is sustainably certified. records.content: Spain A major wine-producing country in southern Europe, known for Tempranillo, Garnacha and its DO hierarchy; Rioja, Ribera del Duero, Cava and Jerez make up a varied drinks landscape. records.content: Stellenbosch Wine of Origin district in the Coastal Region of the Western Cape, South Africa, about 45 km east of Cape Town. The town was founded in 1679 by Simon van der Stel, the country's first wine route opened in 1971 and the WO scheme was instituted in 1973, when Stellenbosch became a legal district. Its vineyards are about 18% of the national 101,957 hectares, with Simonsberg, Helderberg and granite or sandstone slopes creating diverse terroirs. Cabernet Sauvignon is the leading red and Chenin Blanc the main white. WO rules require 100% origin and 85% for variety or vintage claims. It is often mistaken for another name for bourbon, but the two do not fully overlap: Tennessee whiskey has its own conditions in state law, yet it is not listed as a separate class in federal rules. Pinot Noir dominates, first planted in 1965, alongside Pinot Gris, Chardonnay and Riesling. There are 11 nested AVAs, and Oregon requires 90% for a variety label against the federal 75%. Grain, qu starters, fuel and finished liquor could move by water and road, and Yibin became a long-standing commercial node in southern Sichuan. records.content: Bordeaux AOC Decree Bordeaux is a regional appellation, recognised in 1936, with a specification approved in September 2025. records.content: Burgundy AOC Decree Burgundy has 84 appellations in three tiers — regional, village and grand cru — with parcels traced down to historical units called climats. records.content: EU Wine Regulation 1308/2013 The European Union's framework for the common organisation of the wine market. Adopted in December 2013 and applicable from January 2014, it harmonises planting authorisations, geographical indications, labelling and trade. It does not tell a winemaker how to ferment; it defines when a wine may use a name, and what the bottle must disclose. EU Wine Regulation 1308/2013 Europe's wine rules are often read as a recipe book. records.summary: Germany's wine law was last overhauled in 2021, with a new origin hierarchy applying from the 2026 harvest. It keeps four quality tiers and six Prädikat levels
records.content: German Wine Law Germany's wine law was last overhauled in 2021, with a new origin hierarchy applying from the 2026 harvest. It keeps four quality tiers and six Prädikat levels while shifting emphasis from ripeness to place, organised around 13 Anbaugebiete. German Wine Law German wine law is often reduced to a sugar-scale system. That is only half true. Ripeness underpins the Prädikat hierarchy, but the 2021 reform shifted the centre of gravity toward origin: from the 2026 harvest, the geographical tier on the label will say more about a bottle than "Kabinett" or "Spätlese". records.content: Italian DOCG System DOCG is the top tier of the Italian wine pyramid. Created with the DOC system in 1963 and first awarded in 1980, it requires at least 7 years as a DOC, bottles of no more than 6 litres, batch-by-batch chemical and sensory testing, and a state seal. Italian DOCG System On an Italian label, DOCG is the highest statutory tier. It is not a guarantee of the best taste but a set of the strictest production and testing conditions: lower yields, longer ageing, smaller bottles and batch-by-batch chemical and sensory review. records.content: Japan's Liquor Tax Law Japan's Liquor Tax Law (Law No. 6 of 1953) is the national statute that defines liquor, classifies it, requires manufacturing licences and imposes liquor tax; tax is levied by volume on each category and alcohol strength, and a new National Tax Agency rate table applies from 2026-10-01. It is not a labelling law and not the sake grading system. Japan's Liquor Tax Law Japan's Liquor Tax Law (酒税法, Law No. 6 of 1953) is a statute enacted by the Japanese parliament. It defines what “liquor” is, how it is classified, what licences are needed to manufacture and sell it, and how liquor tax is imposed. records.content: Japanese Sake Labelling Japan's National Tax Agency set the standards for sake quality labelling in 1989 by Notification No. 8. Eight specific names separate junmai, ginjo and honjozo styles, tied to polishing ratios, koji share and a cap on added brewing alcohol. The names are process claims, not a ladder of quality. Japanese Sake Labelling The words "junmai daiginjo", "honjozo" and "ginjo" on a sake bottle are not adjectives invented by the brewery. They are "specific names" prescribed by the National Tax Agency. Notification No. 8 of 22 November 1989 established the rules, and later amendments produced today's labelling system. records.content: Tequila NOM-006 Mexican Official Standard NOM-006-SCFI-2012 sets the conditions for using the name tequila: one agave species, a protected territory of 181 municipalities, and certification by the Tequila Regulatory Council. records.content: German Beer Purity Law On 23 April 1516 the Dukes of Bavaria issued an edict at Ingolstadt limiting beer to barley, hops and water. Its principle now sits in section 9 of the German Provisional Beer Law, making it one of the few early-modern ingredient rules still enforced. German Beer Purity Law "German beer may only be brewed from water, malt, hops and yeast." The line is repeated at every beer table, but it is not a statute transported intact from 1516. The 1516 text names only barley, hops and water; yeast joined the list later, and the rule is enforced today through the 1993 Provisional Beer Law. records.content: Spanish DO System Spain's Denominación de Origen system was set by the 2003 vine and wine law, with DO, DOCa, VP and IGP tiers. The framework comes from the vine and wine law of 10 July 2003, Ley 24/2003, which replaced the old statute of 1970. records.content: US AVA System American Viticultural Areas are the US geographical label system for wine, created in 1978 with the first AVA approved in 1980. An AVA only draws a boundary; it does not regulate varieties, yields or winemaking. To name an AVA, at least 85% of the grapes must come from it. US AVA System The AVA is the most misunderstood piece of American wine regulation. Many drinkers assume it works like a French AOC or an Italian DOCG. In fact it does one thing: it draws a boundary around a grape-growing area and gives it a name. It does not dictate varieties, cap yields or require a method. records.content: Abbey beer An umbrella term for beers brewed by monasteries or brewed commercially under a monastery name and licence; Trappist beer must be brewed inside a Trappist monastery under monastic supervision, while abbey beer is mostly a licensed commercial product, and dubbel, tripel and quadrupel denote strength tiers rather than separate styles. records.content: Absinthe A high-strength spirit built on wormwood, fennel and anise and made by maceration and distillation; EU flavouring law sets 35 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg thujone ceilings, and the clouding on dilution is physics, not proof of hallucination. Absinthe Absinthe is a spirit defined by wormwood, fennel and anise. It is normally macerated and distilled, very high in alcohol, and turns milky when water is added. It became central to café culture in France and Switzerland at the end of the 19th century, was banned by several countries in the early 20th century, and only returned to the market from the 1990s. records.content: Altbier A traditional top-fermented beer of Düsseldorf, copper-brown with medium-high hop bitterness and clean malt; cold-conditioned after fermentation, it sits between ale and lager. Altbier Altbier is a traditional top-fermented beer from Düsseldorf and the Rhineland in Germany, conditioned cold like a lager after fermentation. Copper-brown, clean-malted and medium-hopped, it sits between ale and lager; the name Alt means "old", referring to the upper-fermentation method that predated lager brewing. records.content: Amaretto An Italian almond-flavoured sweet liqueur whose name means “slightly bitter”; often infused with almonds, apricot kernels or peach pits, with almond, vanilla, caramel and floral notes, usually 20–28% alcohol. Amaretto Amaretto is an Italian almond-flavoured sweet liqueur whose name comes from amaro, the Italian word for bitter, referring to the slightly bitter finish that kernel ingredients leave behind. It is usually infused with apricot kernels, bitter almonds or peach stones, with almond, vanilla, caramel and floral notes; alcohol is commonly 21–28%, and it can be drunk neat, on ice, or mixed into coffee and cocktails. records.content: Amaro The Italian family of herbal bitter liqueurs, made by macerating or distilling herbs, roots, bark and citrus and blending with syrup; usually 11% to 30% ABV, bittersweet, and used both as a digestif and as a mixing ingredient in Negroni, Manhattan variations and highballs. Amaro Amaro is the Italian family of herbal bitter liqueurs. What they share is not one plant but a structure: herbs, roots, bark, flowers and citrus are macerated or distilled in alcohol to make a bitter base, then blended with syrup, water or spirit so that bitter and sweet balance. records.content: Aquavit A Nordic spirit flavoured with caraway or dill, clear or amber from oak ageing; it belongs to the Christmas table and snaps culture rather than to the vodka family. Aquavit Aquavit, written akvavit or akevitt in the Nordic countries, is a Scandinavian spirit built around caraway seed or dill. It may be clear and colourless or amber from oak ageing, and it usually starts at 37.5% ABV, with 40% a common bottling strength. It is not vodka with flavouring, nor a northern variant of gin: the caraway-dill pairing, the grain or potato base, and the snaps ritual at the Christmas table together define it. records.content: Armagnac A grape brandy from Gascony, protected since 1936, traditionally made in a continuous still that gives roughly 52% to 60% ABV spirit with a broad, weighty aroma; it is divided into Bas-Armagnac, Ténarèze and Haut-Armagnac and keeps a strong vintage tradition. Armagnac The easiest thing to remember about Armagnac is its still: the wine passes through once, not twice as in Cognac. That single pass leaves more congeners behind, gives a lower-strength spirit, and makes the aroma broader, heavier and quicker to show itself. Around this "one pass" technique, Gascon producers built a tradition of bottling single vintages, so each year's weather can be preserved on its own. Armagnac image F

Awamori The recipe for awamori is startlingly short: rice, black koji, water, yeast. There is no second mash addition, no continuous still, no cool slow fermentation to build perfume. Yet this simple sequence has run in Okinawa's heat and humidity for centuries, and it produced a tradition few other Japanese spirits share: sealing the spirit in clay jars and waiting three, ten or thirty years for it to become kusu, "old sake". The traditional method roasts the agave hearts in underground pits, crushes them with stone, ferments the juice and pot-distils twice. records.content: Bock A malt-driven strong lager from Einbeck that Munich brewers reshaped into a dark Bavarian specialty, spanning traditional bock, doppelbock, maibock and eisbock. Bock Bock is a dark, malt-forward strong lager from Germany: full-bodied, low in bitterness and sweet at the finish, associated with late winter and spring. Cider Cider is an alcoholic drink made by fermentation of apple juice. The ingredients are simple, but the range is wide: from tannic, slightly earthy dry cider in western England to sweeter, sparkling farmhouse cider in Normandy, and further to ice cider made from concentrated apple juice in Quebec. Fortified wine Fortified wine is wine to which grape spirit has been added, raising alcohol content and changing the flavour direction. Fruit may be added at mashing, the boil, primary fermentation, secondary fermentation or before bottling, and the range runs from low-alcohol refreshing mixes to complex aged lambics. Fruit Brandy / Eau-de-vie Fruit brandy, or eau-de-vie (literally "water of life" in French), is a clear spirit made by fermenting fresh fruit or juice and then distilling it. Unlike grape-based brandy or pomace distillates such as marc, its raw material is whole fruit or juice, and the aroma comes from the fruit itself. Fruit wine Fruit wine is an alcoholic drink made by fermenting fruit juice or fruit extract with yeast. It is usually lower in alcohol than a distilled spirit, and its flavour depends on the fruit variety, ripeness, fermentation and residual sugar. Genever Genever, or jenever in Dutch, is a grain spirit flavoured with juniper, made mainly in the Netherlands, Belgium and the northern French departments of Nord and Pas-de-Calais. Its technical skeleton is "neutral alcohol plus a botanical blend plus distillation"; its flavour skeleton is "juniper-led with the other botanicals modifying it". Gueuze Gueuze, also written geuze, is a type of Belgian beer made by blending lambic of different ages, bottling the blend and letting residual sugar referment in the bottle. It is not a beer with acid added; it joins the structure of young and old beer: the young supplies fermentable sugar and active yeast, the old supplies acidity, barnyard notes and complexity. records.content: Honey Wine An alcoholic drink fermented from honey and water; honey is nitrogen-poor, acidic and very concentrated in sugar, so fermentation differs from wine, with alcohol from about 3% to over 18% and sweetness set by residual sugar. Honey Wine Honey wine (mead) is an alcoholic drink made by fermenting honey and water with yeast. Ice Wine Ice wine, called Eiswein in German, is a sweet wine made from grapes that freeze naturally on the vine, and it belongs to the wider family of dessert wine. records.content: Imperial Stout The strongest branch of the stout family, descended from the high-alcohol, heavily hopped black beer that Britain exported to Russia in the 18th century; its boundaries are deep roasted grain, a full body, alcohol warmth and long ageing potential, with modern barrel-aged variants. Imperial Stout Imperial stout is the strongest branch of the stout family within beer. It descends from the strong, heavily hopped black beer that Britain exported to the Russian court and the Baltic markets in the 18th century, which is why it is often written as Russian Imperial Stout. records.content: India pale ale A top-fermented beer family defined by prominent hop aroma and bitterness, rooted in British export trade to India and now split into English, American and hazy branches, where bitterness is a variable rather than a grade. India pale ale India pale ale (IPA) is a top-fermented beer family defined by prominent hop aroma and bitterness. It grew out of the British trade in beer exported to India, took a stable form in Burton and elsewhere in the 19th century, and was redefined by American craft brewing in the late 1970s, spawning American IPA, double IPA and hazy IPA. It is protected as a geographical indication in the European Union, and its name carries an extra "e" that separates it in spelling from Scotch and Japanese whisky. Japanese whisky Japanese whisky has a history of less than a century, yet it has acquired a clear international identity. It began by copying Scotland, then developed its own mix of stills, yeast management and mizunara oak. records.content: Kölsch Cologne's pale top-fermented beer, cold-conditioned and filtered, marked by clean fruit, soft bitterness and service in 0.2-litre Stangen, with a geographically protected name. Kölsch Kölsch is a pale, top-fermented beer from Cologne (Köln) in Germany, cold-conditioned and filtered, with a light body, a dry finish and a delicate fruitiness balanced by clear hop bitterness. Technically it is an ale; sensorially it sits close to lager. That combination of warm primary fermentation and cold storage is the key to understanding it, and the name is protected by a geographical indication, so not every pale ale may be called Kölsch. records.content: Lager An umbrella term for beers made with cool bottom-fermenting yeast and then stored near freezing; pale lager, dark lager and Pilsner all belong to it, and lager is a process family while Pilsner is a specific style. Lager Lager is an umbrella term for beers made with cool bottom-fermenting yeast and then stored for a long period near freezing point. Together with top-fermented ale it forms one of the two basic technical routes in brewing. Within the style system of beer, lager is a process family rather than a single style: pale lager, dark lager and Pilsner all belong to it, and Pilsner is merely its most representative branch. Navy Rum Navy rum is the traditional name for the British Royal Navy's daily rum ration; on the modern market it also means a category of high-strength, dark, full-bodied Caribbean blended rum with caramel, spice and dried-fruit notes. records.content: Old Ale / Brown Ale Two adjacent British dark ales: old ale is malty with dried fruit and oxidative notes and is often aged; brown ale is lighter with nuts and caramel and is an everyday ale. Old Ale / Brown Ale Old Ale and Brown Ale are two adjacent directions within traditional British ale: Old Ale is a stronger, malt-sweet, cellared or bottle-aged strong ale, while Brown Ale is a medium-strength everyday British ale built on malt toast and caramel. Both share British malt, traditional ale yeast and low hop bitterness as their base. Old Ale / Brown Ale Figure: Thematic illustration for Old Ale / Brown Ale. records.content: Old Tom Gin A sweetened gin style popular in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century England, made by adding sugar or sweet botanicals such as liquorice after distillation; it is not a legal category, and modern revivals usually sit at 40% to 45% ABV as the historical base for Tom Collins and Old Fashioned variations. Old Tom Gin Old Tom gin is a sweetened gin style popular in England in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Its definition lives in history rather than law: sugar, syrup or sweet botanicals such as liquorice are added to a distilled gin, making the body rounder, softer and easier to drink than the later London Dry. records.content: Ouzo Greece's anise spirit, defined by aniseed, distillation and the milky cloud that appears when water is added; the EU protects the name as a geographical indication, with a minimum strength of 37.5% ABV. Ouzo Ouzo is Greece's most recognisable anise spirit: clear and colourless, it turns milky when water or ice is added, and it tastes of aniseed, liquorice and a faint sweetness, with a herbal bitter edge at the end. It is usually distilled in copper, built around aniseed, and bottled at no less than 37.5% ABV. records.content: Pale Ale A family of pale-malt, top-fermented beers with clearly readable hop aroma; English versions lean on malt and floral hops, American versions on citrus and resinous hops, forming a continuum with bitter and IPA rather than three isolated boxes. Pale Ale Pale ale is a family within beer built on pale malt, top fermentation and clearly readable hop aroma. At one end sits the bitter and cask ale tradition of English ale; at the other, the American Pale Ale that craft brewers rebuilt in the 1980s with Cascade and similar hops. records.content: Perry A low-alcohol drink fermented from pear juice; English perry from the Three Counties is known for high-tannin pear varieties and a bittersweet structure, and it is not the same as apple cider with pear flavouring. Perry Perry is a low-alcohol drink made by fermenting pear juice, most characteristically in Herefordshire, Gloucestershire and Worcestershire in the English West Midlands. It uses purpose-grown, high-tannin pears and ranges from dry to medium-sweet, usually between 4% and 8% ABV. records.content: Pilsner A pale lager born in Plzeň, Czechia, defined by very soft water, Saaz hops, pale malt and cool bottom fermentation, and central to understanding modern pale lagers. Pilsner Pilsner is a pale lager originating in the Bohemian city of Plzeň (Pilsen) in Czechia, characterised by very soft water, Saaz hops, pale malt and cool bottom fermentation. It is both a specific historical style and, in many countries, a loose term for pale lager; the two uses should be kept apart. Within the family of beer, it belongs to the lager branch. records.content: Pisco A grape spirit distilled from freshly fermented juice in Peru and Chile, with separate protected appellations and production rules: Peru requires a single distillation, no added water, sugar or oak, while Chile permits oak maturation and sets strength tiers. Pisco Pisco is a grape spirit distilled from freshly fermented grape juice, produced in Peru and Chile. It belongs to the wider brandy family, yet it follows a different logic from Cognac or Armagnac: most Pisco is never aged in oak, and it is not diluted with water before bottling. records.content: Plymouth Gin A gin style identified with the English city of Plymouth and produced at the Black Friars distillery; softer and earthier than London Dry, the standard bottle is 41.2% ABV and Navy Strength is 57% ABV, and it is a historical base for Pink Gin and the dry Martini. Plymouth Gin Plymouth Gin is a gin identified with the English city of Plymouth. What makes it unusual is not the botanical recipe but the origin rule: the name is tied to the Black Friars distillery in Plymouth, and production moved out of the city cannot be called Plymouth Gin. It is softer and earthier than London Dry, and its history is closely tied to the Royal Navy and classic cocktails.Plymouth Gin image Figure:

records.title: Port

records.content: Port A sweet fortified wine from Portugal's Douro Valley, made by adding grape spirit mid-fermentation and bottled at about 19%–20% ABV, with styles ranging from Ruby and Tawny to Vintage, LBV, Colheita and Crusted. Port Port is a sweet fortified wine from Portugal's Douro Valley. Grape spirit is added before fermentation finishes, killing the yeast, stopping fermentation and leaving sugar in the wine while raising strength to about 19%–20% ABV. Sweet, full-bodied and long-lived is the immediate impression, but the real style split comes after fortification: whether the wine matures in a reductive or an oxidative environment. records.content: Porter A dark top-fermented beer that arose in 18th-century London, given roast, coffee and cocoa flavours by brown malt and later roasted malt; named after market porters and related to stout, though not the same, with modern robust and Baltic porter branches. Porter Porter is a dark top-fermented beer that arose in 18th-century London, with roast, coffee and cocoa flavours coming from brown malt and later roasted malt. The name is said to come from London street and market porters, who were among its main drinkers. Porter and stout share a historical root, but they are not equivalent in strength, sweetness or recipe. Red Brick Porter bottle and a glass of dark beer Figure: A bottle of Red

records.content: Pulque A low-alcohol drink from central Mexico made by fermenting agave sap (aguamiel), usually 4% to 6% ABV; it is neither distilled nor aged, tastes sour, viscous and yeasty, and is served in pulquerías as white pulque or fruit-flavoured curado. Pulque Pulque is a low-alcohol drink from central Mexico made by fermenting agave sap naturally. Its key fact can be stated in one sentence: it is not distilled. The agave is cut and scraped to release sap, the sap ferments in a vessel with wild yeasts and bacteria, and within days it becomes a sour, viscous, yeasty white drink. It shares a plant starting point with tequila and mezcal, but belongs to a completely different technical tradition.Pulqu

records.content: Raicilla A traditional agave spirit from coastal and mountain Jalisco, Mexico, with materials and methods varying by village; smoky, herbal, citrus and mineral, protected by Mexican appellation of origin since 2019 and listed in the EU–Mexico spirit-drinks agreement since 2020. Raicilla Raicilla is an agave spirit distilled in mountain villages and coastal settlements of western Jalisco, Mexico. It belongs to the same agave-spirit family as mezcal, but its wild agave varieties, village-level methods and flavour range are more dispersed. It received Mexican appellation-of-origin protection in 2019 and was added to the EU–Mexico spirit-drinks mutual-recognition list in 2020. Raicilla Figure: T

records.content: Rauchbier A German beer built on beechwood-smoked malt, best preserved in Bamberg, with smoke intensity running from delicate to intense across a spectrum rather than a fixed recipe. Rauchbier Rauchbier is a beer whose main flavour comes from smoked malt, most famously in Bamberg, Bavaria. The smoke comes from beechwood fires used to dry the malt, not from smoke flavouring added to the beer; that distinction defines the boundary between it and a dark beer that merely tastes smoky. Traditional examples are dark lagers, but smoke intensity, colour and strength vary from brewery to brewery. Rauchbier image Figure: Rauchbier. records.title: Red wine

records.content: Red wine Wine made by fermenting dark-skinned grapes with their skins to extract colour and tannin; colour, tannin, acidity and alcohol together shape the style, not a vintage or regional label alone. Red wine Red wine is made from dark-skinned grape varieties. Its colour comes from anthocyanins in the skins, and its tannin from skins, seeds and stems. The biggest difference from white wine is not the colour of the raw material but whether the liquid stays in contact with the skins during fermentation: red wine is usually fermented with skins, extracting colour, tannin and aroma during maceration. records.content: Rhum Agricole A rum distilled from fresh sugarcane juice in Martinique, Guadeloupe and other French Caribbean territories, protected by the Martinique AOC since 1996; it skips molasses, tastes of grass, olive, banana and citrus, and its vieux expression ages at least 3 years in oak. Rhum Agricole Rhum agricole is rum made from fresh sugarcane juice that is fermented and distilled directly. records.summary: A baijiu aroma type made mainly from rice with xiaoqu, through semi-solid fermentation, distillation, ageing and blending, with ethyl lactate and beta-phenyleth
records.content: Rice-aroma baijiu A baijiu aroma type made mainly from rice with xiaoqu, through semi-solid fermentation, distillation, ageing and blending, with ethyl lactate and beta-phenylethanol as the main aroma compounds; the current standard is GB/T 10781.3-2025, with a unified 25.0%–68.0% ABV. Rice-aroma baijiu Rice-aroma is the lightest branch of Chinese baijiu: rice is the only material, xiaoqu is the koji, fermentation is semi-solid, distillation uses a pot still, and the aroma is led by ethyl lactate and beta-phenylethanol. records.content: Rice Wine A low-alcohol fermented drink made in China from glutinous rice with a sweet-rice starter, usually seen as jiuniang or laozao; it is sweet, cloudy and weak, and is neither huangjiu nor baijiu. Rice Wine Rice wine is the low-alcohol drink of China made from glutinous rice with a sweet-rice starter, usually seen as jiuniang or laozao: a white or pale yellow cloudy liquid with half-floating grains, sweet and slightly sour, lightly sparkling, and usually only 1% to 15% ABV. It is neither distilled nor aged like huangjiu. Its value lies in freshness, sweetness and rice aroma rather than in vintage. records.content: Rosé Wine A wine made from red grapes with brief skin contact or direct pressing; colour comes from the skins, not sweetness, and OIV residual-sugar thresholds divide dry to sweet into four bands, while Provence, Tavel and rosé Champagne point in different directions. Rosé Wine Rosé is a type of wine made from red grapes, but the juice spends only a short time in contact with the skins, so it takes on a little colour and tannin. It is neither simply “red wine mixed with white wine” nor a sweetness grade; colour depth, aroma and texture depend on the variety, the maceration method, the fermentation temperature and whether residual sugar is retained. records.content: Rum A spirit distilled from sugarcane juice or molasses, with white, aged, dark and agricole styles. Rum Rum is a spirit made by fermenting and distilling sugarcane juice, molasses or sugarcane syrup. Its flavour range is wide: the same word covers a nearly neutral white mixing base and a dark aged spirit with caramel, vanilla and wood. Understanding raw material, still and ageing matters more than memorising a brand for judging style. records.content: Rye Whiskey A whiskey built on rye as its main grain and matured in new charred oak; US rules require at least 51% rye and straight rye needs two years, while Canada treats Canadian Rye Whisky as the same standard as Canadian Whisky, with no minimum rye share. Rye Whiskey Rye whiskey is whiskey built on rye as its main grain. In the United States it comes with a checkable federal threshold: at least 51% rye in the fermented mash, distillation no higher than 160 proof (80% ABV), barrel entry no higher than 125 proof (62.5% ABV), new charred oak, and bottling at no less than 80 proof (40% ABV). records.title: Saison
records.summary: A farmhouse ale brewed in the cool season in Wallonia and kept for summer farm work; it is defined by high attenuation, a dry finish and peppery, citrusy yeast
records.content: Saison A farmhouse ale brewed in the cool season in Wallonia and kept for summer farm work; it is defined by high attenuation, a dry finish and peppery, citrusy yeast aroma, and modern versions range from low-alcohol everyday beers to strong saisons above 8%. Saison Saison is a beer brewed by Walloon farmhouses in Belgium during the cool season and kept for the summer farm work. It is defined not by colour but by fermentation and palate: high attenuation gives a dry finish, yeast produces pepper, citrus and hay-like aroma, and carbonation is usually lively. Historically it was a low-alcohol drink for farm labour; today it ranges from everyday versions to strong saisons above 8%.Saison image

records.content: Sake A Japanese fermented rice drink made with rice, water, koji and yeast, classified by polishing ratio and brewing method. records.content: Sambuca An Italian anise-flavoured sweet liqueur based on star anise, sugar and neutral spirit; the classic bottling is clear, with deep-blue or red coloured variants; often served with coffee beans or diluted to cloud, usually 38–42% alcohol. Sambuca Sambuca is an Italian anise-flavoured sweet liqueur, led by star anise and built on sugar and neutral spirit. Its legal minimum strength is 38% ABV; the classic bottling is clear, traditionally served with coffee beans or diluted to cloud, mostly as a digestif after meals. records.content: Sauternes The botrytised sweet white of southern Bordeaux, based on Sémillon with Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle; autumn fog from the Ciron river feeds noble rot, while the 1855 classification and the unique status of d'Yquem shaped its reputation. Sauternes Sauternes is the botrytised sweet white of southern Bordeaux, in the Gironde, and one of the easiest sweet wines in the world to name. Its identity is not a single estate but the result of a small river, a fungus and a classification working together. records.title: Scotch whisky
records.summary: Whisky produced in Scotland under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009, in five categories: single malt, single grain, blended malt, blended grain and blended Sco
records.content: Scotch whisky Whisky produced in Scotland under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009, in five categories: single malt, single grain, blended malt, blended grain and blended Scotch; it must mature in oak for at least three years, bottle at no less than 40% ABV and distil at below 94.8% ABV. Scotch whisky Scotch whisky is one of the few spirits that writes where, from what, how, for how long and at what strength into law. Its identity rests not on marketing adjectives but on a series of checkable thresholds: made in Scotland, water and malted barley, at least three years in oak, bottled at no less than 40% ABV, distilled at below 94.8% ABV. records.content: Scottish Ale A traditional Scottish ale, malty and full-bodied with low hop bitterness, caramel, toast and dried fruit; it ranges from the light 60/- to the heavy Wee Heavy. Scottish Ale Scottish ale is the umbrella for Scotland's traditional top-fermented beers, malt-led with low hop bitterness and caramel, toast, toffee and dried-fruit notes. records.content: Sherry A fortified wine from the Jerez region of Spain, based mainly on Palomino and shaped either by biological ageing under flor (Fino, Manzanilla) or oxidative ageing (Oloroso, Amontillado, PX), then blended through the solera system. Sherry Sherry is a fortified wine from the Jerez region of southern Spain. Its distinguishing feature is not simply that alcohol is added, but what happens afterwards. One path runs under a film of yeast called flor, producing the pale, bone-dry, bread-and-almond style of Fino. records.content: Japanese shochu A Japanese distilled spirit under the liquor tax law, split into continuously distilled class A (under 36%) and single-distilled class B (up to 45%); honkaku shochu is made from rice, barley, sweet potato or other materials through koji, two-stage mashing and pot distillation, commonly 25% ABV, and is distinct from both Korean soju and Okinawan awamori. Japanese shochu Japanese shochu is not one drink but a branch of distilled spirits under Japan's liquor tax law. records.content: Single Malt Scotch Whisky A whisky distilled at one Scottish distillery from 100% malted barley in pot stills and matured in oak for at least three years; the 94.8% distillation ceiling and the 40% bottling floor mark its boundary from single-cask and cask-strength releases. Single Malt Scotch Whisky Single Malt Scotch Whisky is one of the five legal categories of Scotch whisky: whisky distilled at a single distillery from 100% malted barley in pot stills, in batches, and matured in oak in Scotland for at least three years. records.content: Single Pot Still Whiskey An Irish whiskey category distilled in pot stills from a mash of malted and unmalted barley; one distillery, a 30% to 30% raw-material split, a 3-year minimum and a 94.8% distillation ceiling define it. Single Pot Still Whiskey Single pot still whiskey is the one Irish whiskey category built on mashing malted and unmalted barley together. The two qualifiers in the name are precise: single means one distillery, and pot still means a pot still. It says nothing about a single cask and nothing about single malt. It is often placed next to mezcal, but the two do not use the same plant: mezcal uses agave, while sotol uses Dasylirion, a genus in the asparagus family. records.content: Sour beer A category of beers given marked acidity by lactic or acetic fermentation; Belgian lambic and red-brown ales, German Berliner Weisse and Gose each form a tradition, and modern kettle souring makes production more controllable, with acidity a style axis rather than a defect or a grade. Sour beer Sour beer is a category of beers in which microbial metabolism produces marked acidity and acidity itself is central to the style. The acid comes mainly from lactic fermentation, and sometimes from acetic fermentation; the organisms involved are not only brewer's yeast but also lactic acid bacteria, acetic acid bacteria and Brettanomyces. records.content: Sparkling wine Wine containing carbon dioxide of fermentative origin that keeps bubbling after opening; traditional method, tank method and ancestral method are distinct, and Champagne is only one example. Sparkling wine Sparkling wine is wine that contains carbon dioxide and keeps producing bubbles after the bottle is opened. The bubbles may come from fermentation or from added gas. Under the OIV definition, true sparkling wine derives its carbon dioxide entirely from fermentation (endogenous origin) and has an excess pressure in the bottle of at least 3.5 bar at 20 °C. records.content: Spiced Rum A flavoured spirit made by adding spices, sugar and caramel to a rum base; common notes are vanilla, cinnamon, clove, nutmeg and orange peel, with styles from light to sweet and rich. Styles run from light and spicy to sweet and vanilla-heavy; alcohol is commonly 35–40%, and it is a common product in Caribbean drinking and modern cocktails. records.content: Stout A top-fermented dark beer given colour and coffee-cocoa flavour by roasted barley, named after stronger porter, represented by Dublin dry stout and split into sweet, oatmeal and imperial stout. Stout Stout is a dark top-fermented beer, characterised by the coffee, cocoa and roast aromas that roasted barley brings. The name comes from 18th century “stout porter”, a stronger porter; in the 19th century Dublin developed the dry stout form, and in the 20th century sweet stout, oatmeal stout and imperial stout branched off. records.content: Tennessee whiskey A Tennessee-produced American whiskey with a corn-led mash, new charred oak maturation and maple-charcoal filtration before ageing, often labelled straight. Tennessee whiskey Tennessee whiskey is often dismissed as bourbon with a different label, which is the laziest way to read it. The grain recipe and the new charred barrels are indeed close to bourbon, but US federal standards give this name its own origin rule and require the new spirit to pass through sugar maple charcoal before it enters the barrel. records.content: Tequila A Mexican spirit distilled from blue Weber agave, with 100% agave and mixto expressions and several age tiers. Its flavour comes from the sweetness and vegetal character of cooked agave hearts, and its process relies on four steps: cooking, crushing, fermentation and distillation. Tokaji Tokaji is the sweet wine of the Tokaj region in north-eastern Hungary, and one of the earliest sweet wine systems to be written into law. Its core is Aszú: botrytised grapes are picked by hand, macerated in base wine or fermenting must from the same vintage, then pressed, fermented and aged in oak for at least eighteen months. records.content: Triple Sec A clear orange liqueur made by macerating sweet and bitter orange peels in neutral spirit, distilling and sweetening; it is a style, not a brand, and its border with curaçao lies in base spirit, colour and sweetness. Triple Sec Triple sec is a clear orange liqueur made by steeping sweet and bitter orange peels in neutral spirit, distilling the infusion and adding sugar. It is neither a protected trademark nor a single brand, but a style that took shape in nineteenth-century France and later became a fixture of cocktail culture. records.content: Umeshu A Japanese sweet liqueur made by steeping green ume plums, sugar and alcohol together without fermentation; "honkaku umeshu" is an industry labelling standard requiring only ume, sugar and alcohol. Umeshu Umeshu is a Japanese sweet liqueur made by steeping green ume plums, sugar and alcohol together in a jar. It is not fermented: the alcohol comes from the base spirit, the plums supply acidity, aroma and colour, and the sugar rounds the sourness. The result is usually pale gold to amber, 10% to 15% ABV, sweet-sour on the palate and marked by almond and honey notes. Vermouth Vermouth is an aromatised wine: a wine base plus wormwood, clove, cinnamon, citrus peel and other botanicals, fortified according to product type and adjusted for sugar. It has the acidity and fruit of wine and the bitterness and aroma of a spirit, so it can be drunk alone or used in cocktails. records.content: Vin Santo A sweet Tuscan “holy wine” made from dried grapes and aged in wood for years; dried apricot, honey, nuts and caramel, traditionally served with cantucci almond biscuits. Vin Santo Vin Santo is a dried-grape wine of central Italy, above all Tuscany: grapes are dried in a ventilated space to concentrate sugar, fermented slowly, then aged for years in small wooden casks. Vodka Vodka is a neutral spirit made from agricultural materials such as grain, potato or molasses, then fermented, distilled and filtered or treated. Wheat beer Wheat beer is top-fermented beer in which wheat makes up a large share of the grain bill. German wheat beer is marked by clove and banana esters and bottle conditioning; Belgian witbier is seasoned with orange peel and coriander; American wheat ale is cleaner and more easy-drinking. records.content: Whisky A grain spirit distilled, then aged in oak, with Scottish, Irish, American and Japanese traditions and strict labelling rules. Whisky Whisky (spelled whiskey in Ireland and the United States) is a spirit made from grain by mashing, fermentation and distillation, then aged in oak. Grain, still, cask and local climate shape the flavour; regional rules determine which names such as "Scotch" and "bourbon" may legally be used. Whisky image Figure: Whisky. records.content: White wine Wine made from white grapes, or from destemmed dark grapes, usually without skin fermentation; acidity, aroma, lees and oak treatment together shape the style. White wine White wine is made from white grape varieties, or from destemmed dark varieties. Unlike red wine, white wine usually does not let the liquid stay in contact with skins for long, so it is pale in colour and low in tannin, with acidity and aroma as its main structural pillars. Its range is wide: from crisp, dry, drink-now wines to rich wines shaped by oak and lees, and to base wines for sparkling wine. records.content: Wine An alcoholic drink made by fermenting fresh grapes or grape must; colour, sweetness, bubbles and regional rules define its categories, while terroir and vintage are only some of the variables. Wine Wine is an alcoholic drink made by fermenting fresh grapes or grape must. The OIV definition requires it to come entirely from fresh grapes (crushed or not) or grape must through partial or complete alcoholic fermentation, with an actual alcoholic strength of at least 8.5% vol. records.content: Yellow wine A traditional Chinese fermented grain wine, mainly rice-based; Shaoxing is its best-known protected origin. records.content: Acidity Acidity describes the amount and strength of acids in a drink, commonly through total acidity in g/L and pH, two different measures; it supports freshness, balance and ageing potential, and affects sulfur dioxide effectiveness. Acidity Acidity image Figure: Acidity. Image: Chemicalinterest, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (source page). records.content: Alcohol by volume (ABV) ABV is the volume fraction of ethanol in a drink measured at 20 °C, usually written as % vol; it is a basic labelling and formulation parameter, not a quality score. Alcohol by volume (ABV) Alcohol by volume (ABV) describes the share of ethanol in a drink by volume. It is usually written as “% vol”: 12.5% vol means that, at 20 °C, every 100 volume units of the drink contain 12.5 volume units of pure ethanol. records.content: Angel's share The angel's share is the portion of a spirit lost through the cask wall during maturation; the Scotch whisky trade often cites about 2% a year, but the real rate depends on temperature, humidity, cask size and warehouse type, and is neither a precise constant nor a quality grade. Angel's share The angel's share is the portion of a spirit that evaporates into the air through the cask wall during maturation. The name is romantic, but the thing it describes is practical: an oak cask is not a sealed container, ethanol and water keep escaping over time, the volume falls and the strength may change. records.content: Appellation An appellation is a legal designation that binds a geographical area to production rules, such as French AOC/AOP, Italian DOC/DOCG, Spanish DO and EU PDO/PGI; it states origin and rules, not a quality ranking. Appellation An appellation is a legal geographical designation: it ties the production of a product to a defined area and a set of rules, and only products made inside that area, under those rules, may use the name. records.content: Aroma Aroma is the volatile smell perceived by the nose, layered by origin into varietal, fermentation and maturation notes; it is not the same as flavour, and aroma is not a synonym for bouquet. Aroma Aroma is the volatile smell perceived by the nose. It is the first piece of information in tasting and a key clue to a drink's type, condition and complexity. Aroma is not the same as flavour: aroma happens mainly in the nasal cavity, while flavour combines taste in the mouth with smell rising from the back of the throat. records.content: Barrel finishing Barrel finishing moves a drink from its main maturation container into a different cask for a further period to add or adjust flavour; it is secondary maturation, not full-term use of that cask, and not cask strength. Barrel finishing Barrel finishing (also called secondary maturation) moves a drink from its main maturation container into a different cask for a further period, to add, adjust or unify flavour. records.content: Brix Degrees Brix (°Brix) express the mass fraction of sucrose in a solution at 20 °C, where 1 °Brix is 1 g of sucrose per 100 g of solution; they measure sugar and soluble solids, not alcohol or sweetness. Brix Degrees Brix (°Brix, also written °Bx) are a unit of sugar concentration. The definition is specific: at 20 °C, 1 °Brix equals 1 gram of sucrose in 100 grams of solution, which is a sucrose mass fraction of 1%. Wine and juice producers use it to judge grape ripeness, estimate potential alcohol and monitor fermentation. Brix image Figure: Brix. records.content: Cask strength Cask strength means whisky bottled with little or no added water, retaining its natural strength from the cask, commonly around 50–65% vol; it is a bottling choice, not single cask or a quality grade. Cask strength Cask strength (also called natural strength) means whisky is bottled with little or no added water, retaining the alcohol by volume the liquid developed in the cask. It describes a bottling decision, not a cask type, an age or a quality grade. Cask-strength products commonly sit around 50%–65% vol, but two batches from the same distillery can differ by several degrees because each cask reaches its own natural strength. Chill filtration Chill filtration is an optional step before bottling whisky: the liquid is cooled close to freezing so that long-chain fatty-acid esters, fatty acids and proteins that were dissolved in the alcohol precipitate, and are then caught by a filter medium. records.content: Clos A clos is a vineyard plot enclosed by a wall, fence or natural boundary, common in Burgundy, the Loire and Alsace; it identifies a bounded site, is not a legal classification, and does not imply single ownership. Clos A clos is a French noun for a vineyard plot enclosed by a wall, fence, ditch or natural boundary. It answers "where is this site and where does it end", not "which quality tier does it belong to". In Burgundy a clos often appears together with a named climat; in the Loire, Alsace, Jura and Champagne it is likewise part of a place name. records.content: Decanting Decanting moves wine from its bottle into another vessel for two purposes — separating sediment and exposing the wine to air; old reds and young tannic wines have different goals, not every wine benefits, and timing depends on age and condition. Decanting Decanting means pouring wine slowly from its bottle into another vessel, usually a wide-bottomed glass decanter. The action has two purposes: separating the wine from sediment at the bottom of the bottle, and letting the wine contact air. Their conditions differ, and treating them as one leads to the mistaken conclusion that every wine should be decanted.Decanting thematic illustration Figure: thematic illustration for Decanting.

records.content: Disgorgement Disgorgement removes the yeast sediment from the neck of a traditional-method sparkling wine after riddling, by hand or with a frozen neck; dosage usually follows before the final closure. Disgorgement Disgorgement (French dégorgement) is the step in traditional-method sparkling wine, after riddling, in which the yeast sediment gathered at the bottle neck is ejected. The sediment comes from the second fermentation in bottle: yeast converts sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide, then dies and forms lees. records.content: Dosage Dosage is the topping liquid added after disgorging traditional-method sparkling wine, usually a blend of base wine and sugar; it replaces the volume lost at disgorging and sets the finished sweetness class, from brut nature to doux under EU rules. Dosage Dosage is the small volume of liquid added to traditional-method sparkling wine after disgorging and before the final closure. It is usually a blend of the same base wine and sugar, known in French as liqueur d'expédition. The step has two jobs: replace the wine lost during disgorging, and set the finished sweetness class. records.content: Dry Dry is a residual-sugar category on wine labels, usually no more than 4 g/L under EU rules and up to 9 g/L when acidity is high; it says nothing about fruit intensity or quality. Dry Dry is the word wine labels use for a very low level of sugar left after fermentation. It answers a narrow question: how much sugar remains? It does not say how intense, good or fruity the wine is. Reading dry as "no fruit" or "top quality" is one of the most common mistakes made at the shelf. records.content: Filtration Filtration passes wine through a medium that physically retains particles and microorganisms; depth and surface filtration differ in structure, and filtration affects clarity, stability and flavour but is not the same as fining. Filtration Filtration passes wine through a medium that physically retains suspended particles, yeast and bacteria. Its immediate aims are clarity and microbiological stability, not "filtering out flavour". records.content: Fining Fining adds bentonite, egg white, gelatin or synthetic polymers to wine so that they adsorb suspended or dissolved targets and settle out, removing protein, tannin, colour or off-flavours; it is a clarification and stabilisation step, not filtration, and raises vegan and allergen questions. Fining Fining is the addition of a small amount of an agent to wine so that it binds suspended or dissolved target substances, forms larger particles and settles, improving clarity and stability. It works through chemical reaction and adsorption; filtration works through physical retention. records.content: Finish Finish is the taste, aroma and mouthfeel that persist after a drink is swallowed or spat out; length, layers and cleanliness determine its quality, and a long finish is not a quality guarantee. Finish Finish (also called length, aftertaste or the tail) is the taste, aroma and mouthfeel that continue in the mouth and nose after a drink is swallowed or spat out. It is not the burst at the moment of swallowing but the fading curve over the following seconds to tens of seconds. In tasting, length, layers, cleanliness and direction together form the judgement, rather than an isolated number of seconds. Finish thematic illustration Figure: thematic illustration for Finish. Flor Flor is the layer of yeast film that forms on the surface of Sherry during biological ageing. In Spanish it is called velo de flor, the "veil of flowers". It is made up of several yeast strains, mainly within Saccharomyces; the film separates the wine from air while metabolising alcohol, glycerol and dissolved oxygen into acetaldehyde and related compounds. records.content: Heads, hearts and tails A distillation run is split by volatility into heads, hearts and tails; hearts are the balanced middle cut and the body of the spirit, while heads and tails carry more impurities and are usually recycled, with cut points shaping style. Heads, hearts and tails Heads, hearts and tails are the three fractions of a pot-still run. They are not three different spirits but three successive parts of one distillation. The operator switches collection vessels according to aroma, taste and strength: heads come first, hearts in the middle, tails last. records.content: Hongqu A purple-red qu made by culturing Monascus on rice; it is a saccharifying starter for huangjiu, a colouring material and a base for red-qu wine and foods, with citrinin risk requiring process control. records.content: IBU (International Bitterness Units) IBU is the unit for beer bitterness, with 1 IBU roughly equal to 1 milligram of iso-alpha acids per litre; it measures hop-derived bitterness, not the bitterness felt on the palate, and not hop aroma. IBU (International Bitterness Units) IBU (International Bitterness Units) is the unit the beer industry uses to quantify bitterness. 1 IBU is roughly 1 milligram of iso-alpha acids per litre of beer, or 1 ppm. It describes the concentration of hop-derived bitter compounds, not the bitterness intensity felt on the tongue at the moment of drinking. Beers at the same IBU can taste completely different because of malt sweetness, carbonation and temperature. IBU

records.title: Late harvest

records.content: Late harvest Late harvest is the practice of leaving grapes on the vine beyond normal ripeness so that water loss concentrates sugar and flavour; it can make sweet wine, but it is not the same as noble rot and not always sweet. Late harvest Late harvest (French vendange tardive) means leaving grapes on the vine beyond normal ripeness and picking them later. In the extra time, the fruit loses water through transpiration, sugar and flavour compounds concentrate, acidity falls, and the berries soften and darken. Late harvest is an important base for sweet and high-alcohol wines, but it is not the same as noble rot and is not necessarily sweeter.Late harvest image Figure: Late harvest. Image: Ag

records.title: Lees

records.content: Lees Lees are the solids, mostly spent yeast plus pulp residue and tartrates, that settle after fermentation; keeping fine lees and stirring them changes texture, aroma and stability. Lees Lees are the solid matter that settles to the bottom of a vessel after fermentation ends. They consist mainly of spent yeast cells, along with grape pulp and skin residue, tartrates, proteins and a little other particulate matter. Lees are not a synonym for dirt, nor waste that must be removed at once; in winemaking they can add flavour and texture, and they can also cause faults. records.content: Maceration Maceration is the contact of juice with skins, pulp, seeds or stems to extract colour, tannin and aroma; time, temperature and alcohol level decide how much, and in which direction, extraction happens. Maceration Maceration is the contact of grape juice with the solid parts, namely skins, pulp, seeds and sometimes stems. It is not a single step but a period of contact that can be placed before, during or after fermentation. records.content: Malolactic fermentation A secondary fermentation in which lactic acid bacteria convert malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide, softening acidity; it differs from alcoholic fermentation and is not needed in every wine. Malolactic fermentation Malolactic fermentation, usually shortened to MLF, is a secondary fermentation in winemaking, but the agent is not yeast. Lactic acid bacteria convert malic acid in the wine into lactic acid and a small amount of carbon dioxide. The result is not alcohol but a change in the structure of acidity. records.title: Mash

records.content: Mash A mash is the mixture of milled malt and hot water in a mash tun, where enzymes convert starch into fermentable sugar. It is the precursor of wort, not wort itself, and its water-to-grist ratio, temperature and pH shape the sugar profile and the extract yield. Mash A mash is the thick mixture of milled malt, or grist, and hot water in a mash tun. It is not wort but the precursor of wort: starch granules gelatinise in the hot water, the malt's amylases cut starch into sugar, proteases break protein down, and a sugar- and amino-acid-rich liquid begins to form. Only the lautering that follows separates that liquid from the spent grain. The state of the mash decides extract yield and sugar

records.title: Mousse

records.content: Mousse Mousse is the formation, bubble size and persistence of the foam in a glass of sparkling wine; bottle pressure is typically about 5–6 bar, and temperature, glassware, wine composition and lees ageing together shape the bubbles, which are not a direct quality score. Mousse Mousse is how the foam behaves after sparkling wine is poured into a glass: how the bubbles start, how coarse or fine they are, how thick the foam layer is and how long it lasts. It is a sensory description, not an analytical result and not a bubble count. Keeping that distinction clear makes it easier to discuss service, wine composition and winemaking separately. records.title: Must

records.content: Must Must is the juice, pulp, skins and solids obtained from crushed or pressed grapes and the starting point of wine fermentation; its sugar, acid, solid content and clarity shape fermentation and style. Must Must is the juice obtained after crushing or pressing grapes, together with the pulp, skins, seeds and a little stem that remain suspended in it. It can be unfermented sweet juice or a fermenting grape mash; in technical usage, must often includes both the liquid and the solid fraction. Must is the starting point of wine, and its sugar, acidity, clarity and solid content determine whether fermentation runs well and where the style will go. Must image Figure: Must. records.title: Noble rot
records.summary: is infection of ripe grapes by Botrytis cinerea under humid nights and dry, sunny days, which shrinks the fruit and concentrates sugar, acid and flavour; it mak
records.content: Noble rot Noble rot is infection of ripe grapes by Botrytis cinerea under humid nights and dry, sunny days, which shrinks the fruit and concentrates sugar, acid and flavour; it makes Sauternes and Tokaji-style sweet wines but differs from grey rot in persistently wet conditions. Noble rot Noble rot is the outcome of Botrytis cinerea infecting ripe grapes under an alternating weather pattern: humid nights and mornings, then dry, sunny afternoons. It is not a separate fungus, and it is not a synonym for "mouldy grapes". The same species causes grey rot when wet weather persists, leaving fruit soft, leaking and off-flavoured. records.content: Original gravity Original gravity is the concentration of soluble solids, mainly sugars and other extract, in wort before fermentation, usually expressed in °P (degrees Plato); it reflects raw-material extract and is not alcohol content. Original gravity Original gravity (OG) is the concentration of soluble solids, mainly sugars and other extract, in wort after mashing and before pitching yeast. It answers "how much extract can this grist provide", not "how much alcohol will the finished beer contain".
